Abhidhamma · Chapter 5

4. Vipāka (result). “When we see, hear, taste, sme (p. 81–84)

Pages 81–84 (4 pages)
Abhidhamma 4. Vipāka (result). “When we see, hear, taste, sme (p. 81–84) p. 81

4. Vipāka (result). “When we see, hear, taste, smell or touch pleasant or unpleasant objects it is result”, the result of a deed in the past. The seeing itself is neither good nor bad. 5. (c) unpleasant feeling. The two kinds rooted in aversion “are accompanied by unpleasant feeling”. Attachment can come with pleasant or indifferent feeling; ignorance with indifferent feeling. 6. Consciousness that is neither cause nor result: it has “no effect in terms of cause and result”. It arises in the sense-door process, in the thought processes of enlightened beings and in nine of the meditative states. 7. (b) māna (conceit). “The characteristic of conceit is haughtiness and self-praise is its function.” 8. Contact, feeling, perception (or memory), intention, concentration, psychic life and attention: phassa, vedanā, saññā, cetanā, ekaggatā, jīvitindriya, manasikāra. 9. False. “Kindness and hate cannot occur together at the same moment, restlessness and balance of mind cannot occur together, compassion and conceit cannot occur together.” 10. (c) 52. “There are 52 different types of cetasikas”: 7 universals, 6 particulars, 14 bad, 19 beautiful, 3 abstinences, 2 illimitables and wisdom. 11. Adosa (non-hate), one of the nineteen beautiful mental factors, when it takes living beings as its object. It is not a person’s feeling; it is a conditioned mental factor that arises and falls away.

Quiz 3 (lessons 5 and 6) 1. (a) 28: 12 gross and 16 subtle. “There are 28 classes of rūpa, 16 being classified as subtle and 12 as gross.” 2. Earth, or solidity; water, or cohesion; fire, or temperature; wind, or motion. In Pāḷi: paṭhavī, āpo, tejo, vāyo. 3. False. “Hardness is a type of rūpa (matter). It cannot know anything about anything.” 4. (b) the eye-sense. The derived rupas are “the physical sense-organs of eye-sense, ear-sense, tastesense, etc., and the sense-objects of colour, sound, smell and flavour”, and others such as heart-base, nutritive essence and space. Seeing, feeling and doubt are nāma (mind). 5. A group of eight: the four great elements, colour, smell, flavour and nutritive essence. Matter never arises as a single kind. 6. (b) the results of deeds done in the past. “Whenever we see, hear, taste, smell or touch an object, that experience … is resultant-consciousness (vipaka-citta). It is the result of a deed performed at some time in the past.” 7. 1. cetanā (intention) arises with a moment of consciousness, as it does with every moment; 2. the intention grows strong enough to move the body or the speech; 3. one of the ten good or bad deeds is done: this is kamma (deed); 4. at some time in the future, a pleasant or unpleasant result arises as seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting or touching. Intention is universal; when it is strong enough to motivate one of the ten kinds of action it is called kamma (deed), “because it is strong enough to produce a result at some time in the future”.

8. “The justification for killing is just thinking, but the actual moment of killing is always immoral and never to anybody’s benefit.” The ten bad deeds, “no matter what the justification that we make for them, are always immoral actions”.

9. (a) rejoicing in others’ merit. The ten are generosity, restraint, mental development, respect, service, sharing of merit, rejoicing in others’ merit, listening to Dhamma, teaching Dhamma and straightening one’s views. 10. The mental factor cetanā (intention). Intention arises with every moment, but “when intention motivates one of the ten types of moral or immoral actions through body, speech or mind then it is called kamma because it is strong enough to produce a result at some time in the future”. 11. False. “Sharing of merit is not practised at all in western countries today. It is something difficult for us to understand since we don’t admit the existence of other realms of beings.” 12. ”… be kind, respectful, generous, honest and upright in character. The Buddha taught quite clearly that it is deeds in the past that determine our life situation right now.”

Quiz 4 (lessons 7 and 8) 1. (c) 31. “The Buddha enumerated 31 planes of existence”: 4 woeful planes, the human plane, 6 planes of devas (heavenly beings) and 20 planes of Brahmās (the highest heavenly beings). 2. The hell realms, the realm of asuras (titans), the realm of petas (unhappy ghosts) and the animal realm. Only the animal realm can be seen by human beings. 3. (b) they are all temporary. “Existence in all of these planes has one thing in common, it is temporary, it does not last.” So “heaven is not the end of it all”. 4. The sticks. If he laid one for each mother, “the straw, boughs, twigs and leaves in this India would come to an end and be used up” before the mothers were counted. There is no beginning to the round of births. 5. 1. a past deed, or a habit, becomes the object of the last thought process; 2. the mind reacts to it with kusala (good) or akusala (bad); 3. cuti-citta (death consciousness), the last moment of this life; 4. paṭisandhi-citta (rebirth consciousness), the first moment of the next life. The last process takes a deed or habit as object; the reaction decides the plane; then death consciousness, then at once rebirth consciousness. There is no gap.

6. False. “Whatever persons surround us or help us they cannot determine our last thought process. It depends upon deeds in the past what happens to us at death.” 7. (b) wrong view, doubt and adherence to rule and ritual. “At the first stage, a being has eliminated the first three fetters”: wrong view, doubt and adherence to rule and ritual. 8. He “has entered the stream to final enlightenment”. “There are no more conditions to be born in a lower plane than that of a human being.” 9. (b) sense desire and aversion. “A never-returner (anagami) eliminates two further fetters, these being sense-desire and aversion. He has no more desire for sense-objects and no more dislike for unpleasant things.” 10. Attachment to existence in the form realms, attachment to existence in the formless realm, conceit, restlessness and ignorance. 11. “When an arahant dies, that is all. No more experience. No more rebirth. This is called by the Buddha the only true peace.” The last moment is not followed by another rebirth consciousness. 12. False. The belief “that there is a method or a technique or something which one performs that will lead one to enlightenment” is itself one of the three fetters cut at the first stage.

Quiz 5 (lessons 9 and 10) 1. (c) ignorance. “We can see then that at the root of it all is ignorance. That is defined as ignorance of the Four Noble Truths.” 2. 1. phassa (contact); 2. vedanā (feeling); 3. taṇhā (craving); 4. upādāna (grasping). Dependent on contact arises feeling; dependent on feeling arises craving; dependent on craving arises grasping.

3. Life is unsatisfactory, dukkha (suffering); suffering arises because of craving; there is an ending of suffering, nibbāna (the end of all troubles); the way to that ending is the Noble Eightfold Path. 4. (b) eight mental factors that arise together in a moment of wisdom. “In the Abhidhamma it is made clear that the Eightfold Path is in fact only momentary phenomena like everything else … at the moment that a wholesome moment of wisdom … arises then it is accompanied by the Eightfold Path factors as mental factors (cetasikas).” 5. “Five of these factors accompany every moment of true wisdom. The whole eight occur together only at the moments of enlightenment.” 6. Dukkha (unsatisfactory: there is no lasting satisfaction in them), anicca (impermanent: they do not last even for a moment) and anattā (non-self: they are all empty of self). 7. (b) body-sense consciousness experiencing hardness, seeing, and memory, each at a different moment. “It is, in fact, a type of (body-sense) consciousness which experiences hardness through the body, seeing which sees and memory which remembers what we are doing … So in reality no ‘person’ exists who is ‘sitting’ on a ‘chair’.” 8. False. “Hardness is not a seat. ‘Seat’ or ‘chair’ are conventional labels we give to other sets of experience through different senses.” 9. “When people insult us, it is just sound appearing through the ear.” The hearing is vipāka (result); the sound is rūpa (matter); the hurt is dosa (anger) arising in a later moment. 10. ”… no person in them. This knowledge as it develops, ultimately brings us release from this unsatisfactory wheel of existence.” 11. (b) the world, its origin, its ceasing and the means to its cessation. “As long as a man is vague about the world, / About its origin, about its ceasing, / About the means that lead to its cessation, / So long he cannot recognise the truths.”

Quiz 6 (lessons 11 and 12) 1. (b) three: greed, hate and delusion. “Three things, sire, happen of that nature. What are the three? Greed, hate, and delusion:—these three make for trouble, for suffering, for distress.” 2. Not “we”: “We cannot eradicate the defilements of others, ‘we’ cannot even eradicate our own defilements. But when right understanding has been developed, it is right understanding which can gradually eradicate defilements. But this may take many lives.” 3. False. “Love is real, but it falls away immediately, and it does not belong to a self who could be master of it.” 4. That there is no master of them: “We can have the intention to be kind, but we cannot force ourselves to kindness. When things are not the way we want them to be we may become angry, in spite of ourselves, as we say. This shows us that phenomena are anatta, not self.”

5. (b) an accumulation of experiences handed on from each moment of consciousness to the next. “There is nothing lasting in a man, not even what we call his character.” But “we can still speak of an ‘accumulation’ of experiences in each moment of consciousness, and we can call this character.” 6. ”… generosity or anger in the future. A moment of right understanding now conditions right understanding in the future, and thus it is possible to develop wisdom.” 7. (b) hardness. “Person, animal, tree or house are not paramattha dhammas, they are concepts.” Hardness is a rūpa (matter) that can be directly experienced through the body-sense. 8. “Seeing sees and it does not think … There is seeing, and seeing sees visible object. Seeing does not see a man or a tree.” Shape and form, and persons, are known by thinking, in later moments. 9. (b) intellectual understanding of what nāma and rūpa are. “The condition for right mindfulness is intellectual understanding of what nama and rūpa are: realities which appear through the six doorways.” Mindfulness “can arise when there are the appropriate conditions”, not because of our will. 10. False. “When one, for example, follows what one’s hands and feet are doing in a day one does not learn anything about nama and rūpa, about what is real, about impermanence.” 11. “Heat or cold, hardness or softness can appear through the body-sense”, “not a person, not my husband”. Of the attachment: “There is attachment and this is real, we do not have to try to suppress it.” 12. “Through the development of insight we will become more patient, we will have more lovingkindness and compassion. Thus, the development of insight is to the benefit of other people as well.” 13. (a) the deathless, the cool, the incomparable, the peaceful. “Nibbāna is described as the ‘deathless’, the ‘cool’, the ‘incomparable’, the ‘peaceful’. It is the end of craving, the goal of the Buddha’s teachings.”
